title: dedicated-pool-degradation-triage-scrapbook
content:
Purpose: informal on-call scrapbook capturing a recurring Dedicated GPU pool degradation event that looks like a combination of noisy-neighbor memory pressure and an autoscaler configuration gap. Intended audience: on-call SREs, infra engineers owning Dedicated, and Platform Eng for policy fixes. This is a working doc — notes, hypotheses, commands we ran, and a first-pass runbook to validate in staging.

High-level summary (TL;DR):
- Symptom: sudden tail-latency spikes and allocation failures for hosted dedicated jobs across pool-03 (us-west-2a) around 2026-02-17 21:13 UTC. CPU on nodes stayed low but GPU memory saturation and driver-level OOMs were observed.
- Root-hypothesis: a combination of an aggressive batch workload from tenant T-psi that launches multi-GPU distributed jobs and an autoscaler downscale-to-zero misconfiguration that left a small set of nodes overloaded (hot shards). Noisy neighbor because tenant jobs were not pinned/isolated and affinity rules allowed co-location of high-memory batch pods with latency-sensitive inference pods.
- Immediate mitigations applied: cordoned 3 nodes, evicted batch pods, applied taint+toleration rules for latency-sensitive daemonset, bumped dedicated-pool min-replicas from 2 to 5, forced rolling eviction of old GPU drivers on 2 nodes.

Detection timeline (evidence aggregated from monitoring, logs, and oncall):
- 21:11 UTC: alert spike - "gpu-memory-pressure-high" fired for pool-03 from prom rule (gpu_mem_util > 92% for 2m).
- 21:12 UTC: support Slack thread started (#sre-incidents). Oncall (Avery) confirmed "inference 503s" being paged from hosted-api.
- 21:16 UTC: kubectl top shows node-level GPU memory 95% on nodes node-a3,node-a4,node-b1. nvidia-smi on node-a3 shows a 4x distributed training group holding 98% of memory on GPU:0 and 3.
- 21:20 UTC: scheduler logs show Pending pods with events "Insufficient gpu" and OOMKills in kubelet logs referencing /var/log/nvidia/driver_error.
- 21:26 UTC: autoscaler logs (horizontal-gpu-autoscaler) show a recent scale-down decision at 20:50 UTC that removed 4 nodes when utilization across the pool was averaged below threshold, but the scaler ignored per-zone hot spots due to metric bucketing.

What we ran (commands & snippets):
- Diagnosing: kubectl get pods -n dedicated --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o wide
- Node checks (via bastion): ssh node-a3 sudo nvidia-smi -q | grep "Memory Usage" -A2
- Driver logs: sudo journalctl -u nvidia-driver | tail -n 200
- Kubelet events: kubectl describe node node-a3 | sed -n '1,200p'
- Autoscaler tail: kubectl logs deploy/gpu-autoscaler -n infra --since=4h | grep scaleDown

Immediate mitigation checklist (what we did and why):
- Cordon/Drain strategy: cordon node-a3,a4,b1 to stop new pods landing and evict batch jobs gracefully (kubectl cordon/evict). Result: 40% reduction in immediate memory pressure.
- Tenant isolation: identified T-psi batch pods via pod labels (tenant: t-psi, job-type: distributed-train). Applied nodeSelector/affinity to pin future batch jobs to pool-spot nodes only (temporary policy).
- Autoscaler config tweak: increased min-replicas for pool-03 from 2 to 5 to avoid dangerous downscales. Filed follow-up to implement per-zone minima.
- Quick scheduler safeguard: created a mutating webhook rule to reject pod creations with gpu.memory_request > 70% unless they have explicit isolation labels. (Temporary, rollback in 2 hours if interferes with customer jobs).
- Observability: added additional dashboard panels showing per-node 95th/99th percentile GPU memory across 10m windows (not just cluster average).

Post-incident root cause analysis (work-in-progress, hypothesis tree):
1) Autoscaler behavior mismatch (probable primary): scaler uses pool-average metrics. When a single heavy job lands on a small number of nodes, the average across the pool underestimates local hotspots -> safe to conclude this allowed downscale decisions that left insufficient capacity.
2) Scheduling affinity gap (secondary): batch jobs lacked strong anti-affinity/taints vs. latency-critical inference pods. Default scheduler bin-packing allowed co-location, which is fine in normal times but not when training jobs request large contiguous GPU memory.
3) Driver/kernel fragility (contributing): older NVIDIA drivers on two nodes showed repeated driver warnings that correlated with OOMs; upgrading reduced frequency of hard OOMs but did not eliminate capacity problem.
4) Insufficient telemetry granularity (enabler): alerting based on average pool utilization masked hotspots; no rule existed to detect uneven per-node skew.

Runbook draft (first-pass actionable steps for oncall):
- Phase 0 (Detection):
  0.1 - Confirm alerts: check prom rule "gpu_memory_pressure_high" and cross-check node-level memory util.
  0.2 - Pager validation: ensure errors correspond to dedicated pool label and not a regional outage.

- Phase 1 (Containment):
  1.1 - Identify top offending pods: kubectl top pods -n dedicated --use-protocol=summary | sort -k3 -nr | head -n 10 (filter for gpu memory if available).
  1.2 - If pod is non-latency batch: evict with grace period 120s; if stateful, coordinate with Solutions Eng. Command: kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force <node>
  1.3 - If pod is latency-sensitive and suffering errors, cordon other nodes and migrate the offending batch pods instead.
  1.4 - If multiple nodes show >90% gpu_mem, bump pool min-replicas and open an emergency scale: kubectl patch hpa/gpu-pool-03 -p '{"spec":{"minReplicas":5}}'

- Phase 2 (Remediation):
  2.1 - Apply temporary taint to pooled nodes: kubectl taint nodes <node> noisy-neighbor=true:NoSchedule for nodes with repeated offenders.
  2.2 - Label relocated nodes for batch-only scheduling: kubectl label node <node> batch-only=true
  2.3 - Trigger rolling restart of nodes with driver warnings: set cordon -> drain -> upgrade driver package -> uncordon. (Follow driver upgrade playbook doc id INF/DRIVER-UPGRADE).

- Phase 3 (Recovery validation):
  3.1 - Verify 95th/99th percentile GPU mem drop on each node for 20m window.
  3.2 - Validate customer latency graphs for hosted-api routes pinned to pool-03.
  3.3 - Re-enable normal scheduling once 30m steady-state is observed and no new scale-down pending.

- Phase 4 (Post-incident):
  4.1 - Roll permanent autoscaler change: require per-zone minima and change metric bucketing to per-node hot-spot detection. Create INF ticket for design.
  4.2 - Add scheduler admission rule: large contiguous GPU memory requests (>60%) require "isolate: true" label or are scheduled only to batch-only nodes.
  4.3 - Driver lifecycle: enforce staggered driver upgrades and monitoring to avoid correlated driver failures.
  4.4 - Follow-up telemetry: Prometheus rule: node_gpu_mem_skew > 30% for 5m -> page oncall + tie to runbook.

Open questions / unresolved items:
- Why did the autoscaler bucket at pool-level only? Design doc suggests zone-aware mode exists but wasn't enabled for this pool. Who flipped it off and when? (related PR: #912).
- Are there customer SLAs impacted where we should proactively notify? We need a CS sync to decide communications for mid-tier customers running on Dedicated.
- How often should we schedule forced preemption windows for batch work to avoid long-lived memory-hogging pods?

Post-incident action items (short list assigned):
- INF-2437 (owner: Priya Nair): implement per-zone minima and adjust metric aggregation to include node-level skew detection.
- INF-2440 (owner: Marcus Valdez): create scheduler policy enforcement for contiguous memory requests (admission webhook + docs).
- INF-2444 (owner: Avery Chen): add new Grafana panels and alert rules for node-level GPU memory skew and 99th percentile node mem across 10m.
- INF-2445 (owner: Platform Eng): run driver upgrade across pool-03 with a 1-node-at-a-time window and verify post-upgrade stability.

Notes for future runbook improvements (ideas):
- Preflight check for new heavy-job submissions: a low-friction "declare" API for jobs to mark themselves as "distributed-large" which triggers scheduler isolation automatically.
- Baked-in soft preemption: support a best-effort graceful shrink for distributed jobs older than X hours.
- Simulation harness to replay historical placement and autoscaler decisions to see what downscale would have done in different configs.

Appendix: useful commands and quick helpers
- List top GPU consumers (namespace): kubectl get pods -n dedicated -o custom-columns=POD:.metadata.name,NS:.metadata.namespace,GPUMEM:.metadata.annotations.gpu_mem_request --sort-by=.metadata.annotations.gpu_mem_request | tail -n 50
- Evict a pod gently: kubectl delete pod <pod> -n dedicated --grace-period=120
- Quick scale patch for HPA: kubectl patch hpa gpu-pool-03 -n infra -p '{"spec":{"minReplicas":5}}'
- Check autoscaler decisions: kubectl logs deploy/gpu-autoscaler -n infra --since=6h | sed -n '1,200p' | grep -i scale

Remember: this file is a working notebook. Convert the runbook section into the canonical SRE-runbooks repo once validated. If you touch autoscaler configs, coordinate with platform-eng and notify CS before rolling out global changes that alter capacity guarantees.

End of scrap notes.
